feat: add new script blocker (#419)

## Overview
Deprecates the tracking blocker in favor of script loading allowing for
full control over what is blocked and what is not.
In the React packages, the script loader can also conditionally render
React components based on the consent. For example if you wanted to load
a script with `Next/Script` or a React Provider instead.

We now also have pre-defined scripts for stuff like Google Tag Manager,
Meta Pixel & Posthog

feat(react): add frame component to conditionally render iframes etc (#420)

## Overview
Core: 
Render iframes based on consent via data-src and data-category tags.
This does not display fallback content.

React: 
Conditionally render components & elements based on the consent. 

We do this in the UI level with react as you want a UI fallback for your
iFrames, to prevent layout shifts and provide better UX. This component
is customizable similar to the other c15t components.

This is useful for iframes such as for youtube embeds as they set
cookies on load or play.

## Related Issue
Fixes #335 

## Type of Change
- [x] 🚀 New feature

## Usage
c15t:
```html
  <iframe
    width="560"
    height="315"
    data-src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/mQJ6q1ZCzsg"
    data-category="marketing" // Note: Not typesafe
  />
```

@c15t/react:
``` tsx
<Frame category="marketing" className="h-[300px] w-[500px]">
	<iframe
		title="Cool Duck Video"
		src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/mQJ6q1ZCzsg"
		width="100%"
		height="100%"
	/>
</Frame>
```

feat(translations): add automated translations with Lingo.dev CLI (#500)

This PR:

- adds support for more EU languages to the `@c15t/translations` package
- sets up [Lingo.dev CLI](https://lingo.dev/en/cli) for easier
generation and maintenance of translations

This approach has a few benefits:

- the translations are generated with AI
- as the source content is updated, only the changes are retranslated
- support additional languages with just a couple of (small) changes

Some other possible enhancements (not in this PR) include:

- translating the documentation (either for all locales or just a
subset)
- setting up CI/CD integration that:
    - verifies if translations have been generated
- commits translations automatically to repo (directly to the main
branch, or via PR, etc)

**Note:** Based on the config in this PR, a Lingo.dev API key is
required. It's also possible to BYOK with a standard LLM provider though
(e.g., OpenRouter).

Fixes https://github.com/c15t/c15t/issues/497

refactor(workflows): consolidate and update deployment workflows (#538)

- Removed outdated workflows for canary, preview, and production
deployments.
- Introduced a new unified deployment workflow to handle various
deployment scenarios including PR previews, scheduled checks, and manual
triggers.
- Enhanced the release workflow to support both canary and regular
releases with appropriate configurations for pnpm and Node.js.
- Improved permissions and concurrency settings for better workflow
management.
## Overview

This PR consolidates and enhances GitHub Actions workflows to improve
maintainability and add new capabilities:

1. **Merged release workflows**: Combined `canary-release.yml` and
`release.yml` into a single unified workflow that handles both canary
and production releases based on branch triggers.

2. **Added PR preview workflow**: Created a new workflow
(`pr-preview.yml`) that automatically detects changed packages in PRs
and publishes preview versions to `pkg.pr.new` for testing before
merging.

3. **Merged docs deployment workflows**: Combined
`deploy-docs-preview.yml` and `deploy-docs-production.yml` into a single
workflow with manual trigger support for both preview and production
deployments.

**Benefits:**
- Reduced workflow duplication and maintenance overhead
- Single source of truth for release and deployment logic
- Better developer experience with PR preview packages
- Manual deployment controls for production/preview environments
- Simplified npm trusted publisher configuration (only one workflow file
needed)

## Type of Change

- [x] 🏗️ Refactor (no functional changes)
- [x] ✨ Enhancement (improves existing functionality)
- [x] 🚀 New feature

## Implementation Details

### Key Changes

1. **Unified Release Workflow** (`.github/workflows/release.yml`)
   - Merged `canary-release.yml` and `release.yml` into single workflow
   - Triggers on push to `main` or `canary` branches
   - Uses conditional steps to handle canary vs production releases
   - Maintains all existing functionality while reducing duplication

2. **PR Preview Workflow** (`.github/workflows/pr-preview.yml`)
   - New workflow for publishing preview packages from PRs
   - Automatically detects which packages changed in PR
   - Only publishes packages with `publishConfig` (published packages)
- Security: Only runs for repository members or PRs with
`deploy:preview` label
   - Publishes to `pkg.pr.new` with version `0.0.0-preview.<SHA>`
   - Adds install instructions as PR notices

3. **Unified Docs Deployment Workflow**
(`.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml`)
   - Merged `deploy-docs-preview.yml` and `deploy-docs-production.yml`
   - Supports automatic deployments on push to `main`/`canary`
   - Added manual `workflow_dispatch` trigger with options:
     - Deployment type: `preview` or `production`
     - Branch selection
     - PR number (for preview deployments)
   - Conditional steps based on deployment type

### Technical Notes

- **Release workflow**: Uses conditional steps with `if` conditions to
determine canary vs production behavior, avoiding duplicate code while
maintaining clear separation of concerns.

- **PR preview workflow**: Uses matrix strategy to build/publish
multiple changed packages in parallel. Package detection uses git diff
to identify changed packages and filters to only published packages.

- **Docs deployment workflow**: Uses a deployment info extraction step
to determine branch/PR context, then conditionally runs preview or
production deployment steps based on trigger type.

- **Workflow consolidation**: All merged workflows maintain backward
compatibility - existing triggers and behaviors continue to work as
before.

fix: add NODE_AUTH_TOKEN for npm publish auth (#686)

## Summary

- Adds `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN` env var (set to `NPM_RELEASE_TOKEN` secret) to
all three release steps (production, canary, RC)
- Fixes the E404 errors that caused all 7 packages to fail publishing at
v1.8.6

## Root Cause

`actions/setup-node@v4` with `registry-url` creates an `.npmrc` at
`$RUNNER_TEMP` that references `${NODE_AUTH_TOKEN}`, and sets
`NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG` to point to it. The changesets action creates
`~/.npmrc` using `${NPM_TOKEN}`, but npm **ignores** it because
`NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG` takes precedence.

Since the workflow only set `NPM_TOKEN` (not `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`), npm was
authenticating with an empty token — resulting in E404 for all publish
attempts.

The previous `npm install -g npm@latest` step (removed in #684) likely
reset the npm config chain, masking this issue. Once that step was
removed, auth broke.

## Test plan
- [ ] Merge to main → release workflow re-runs → 1.8.6 publishes
successfully to npm
- [ ] Verify `npm view @c15t/backend@1.8.6` returns package info after
publish

## Overview

Fix the `@c15t/dev-tools/tanstack` integration so it uses TanStack
Devtools' React plugin API, keeps the c15t store connected across plugin
tab switches, and presents an embedded UI that fits TanStack's dark
styling. This also adds a dedicated demo page for reproducing and
validating the embedded plugin behavior.

### Key Changes
1. Replace the imperative TanStack adapter with a React plugin factory,
expose `c15tDevtools()`, and keep `c15tDevtoolsPlugin` as a
compatibility alias.

embedded mode to match TanStack's dark palette, and add a
`/tanstack-devtools` repro page plus docs/tests for the workflow.

### Technical Notes

The embedded panel now caches its `createDevToolsPanel()` instance by
namespace and only destroys it after a delayed release, which avoids
losing the underlying store connection when TanStack swaps plugin views.
Embedded mode also uses a scoped token override so existing c15t panel
components render with TanStack-like colors without changing the
standalone DevTools theme.

subject endpoints by adding request parameter and request body metadata
to the schemas used by the backend docs generator.

and allowed parameters so users do not need to inspect contract files
manually. In this codebase those docs are generated from route

feat(scripts): add daily live vendor script monitor (#903)

Closes #899

## Summary

Adds a Playwright-based **live vendor probe harness** for every built-in
`@c15t/scripts` integration, plus a daily GitHub Actions monitor that
opens/updates deduped issues when a vendor's live loader behavior breaks
— the class of failure static jsdom tests can't see (like the Microsoft
Clarity loader change).

### How it works

`packages/scripts/live-vendors/` contains a runner that bundles a
browser harness with `Bun.build`, serves it locally, and drives real
Chromium through five phases per vendor:

1. **consent** — with denied consent, the script must not load and no
loader request may leave the page
2. **bootstrap** — queue stubs/globals seeded by the manifest must exist
immediately after `loadScripts()`, before the network answers
3. **load** — the real vendor loader must respond (full tier requires a
2xx JavaScript response; `loader-only` accepts placeholder-id
rejections, including Chromium ORB-filtered error pages)
4. **runtime** — the real vendor SDK must initialize (full tier, polled)
5. **network** — every third-party request outside the loader allowlist
is answered with an empty 204, so probes never send real analytics data

Failed probes retry once; every run writes a JSON report. A registry
coverage test makes CI fail if a vendor is added to the registry without
a live probe config, so future integrations (#873–#881) must ship with
live coverage.

### Workflow

`.github/workflows/script-vendor-monitor.yml` — daily at 06:30 UTC +
`workflow_dispatch` with optional vendor filter. Separate from PR CI so
transient third-party failures never block PRs. Opens one deduped issue
per failing vendor (`[vendor-script-monitor] <vendor> live script
contract failed`), comments while it keeps failing, auto-closes on
recovery. Issue planning logic is pure and unit-tested. zizmor-clean.

### Results

Full sweep: **26/26 vendors pass** — 20 full tier (real SDKs boot from
vendor CDNs: gtag, PostHog, Meta Pixel, TikTok, Intercom, …), 6
loader-only with documented placeholder-id limitations (GTM 404s fake
containers, Clarity answers 204, etc.). Upgrading loader-only vendors to
full tier needs real test-account ids as repo secrets — tracked as a
follow-up.

**The first sweep found a real bug**: the live Mixpanel SDK rejects our
stub with `Mixpanel error: Version mismatch` and never initializes (our
manifest bootstrap lacks the snippet contract, e.g. `__SV`). Fix lands
as a stacked PR.

### Local usage

```sh
bun run --filter @c15t/scripts test:live-vendors
bun run --filter @c15t/scripts test:live-vendors -- --vendor microsoft-clarity
```

fix(scripts): implement Mixpanel snippet contract so the SDK initializes (#905)

Fixes #904. Stacked on #903 (the live vendor monitor that found this
bug).

## Summary

The `mixpanel-analytics` manifest seeded `window.mixpanel = []` with
queue methods but never implemented Mixpanel's snippet contract. The
live SDK checks the snippet version marker and bails with:

```
Mixpanel error: Version mismatch; please ensure you're using the latest version of the Mixpanel code snippet.
```

…so in production the SDK loaded but **never initialized, and queued
`track`/`identify` calls were silently dropped**.

### Fix

The manifest bootstrap now reproduces the official snippet contract
(verified against the unminified `mixpanel-2-latest.js` source):

- `mixpanel.__SV = 1.2` — without it `init_from_snippet` refuses to boot
- `mixpanel._i = [[token, initOptions, 'mixpanel']]` — the pending init
tuple `init_from_snippet` consumes at load. The explicit `'mixpanel'`
instance name is load-bearing: `create_mplib` resolves the queue stub
through `mixpanel_master[name]`, so a two-element tuple makes the SDK
create an orphan instance and leave the stub in place (silently — no
console error)
- the `afterLoad` `mixpanel.init(...)` call is removed; init happens
through the snippet registry like the official snippet

Queued calls already used the right format (`[method, ...args]` arrays),
so they replay correctly via `_execute_array` once init actually runs.

The live probe for mixpanel is upgraded back to **full tier** with a
runtime assertion that the real SDK reports `__loaded` — the monitor now
guards this contract daily.

## Test plan

- [x] `bun run --filter @c15t/scripts test` — 206 tests / 50 files pass
(unit + e2e contract tests updated to assert the snippet contract)
- [x] `bun run --filter @c15t/scripts check-types` / `lint` — clean
- [x] Live probe against the real CDN: `test:live-vendors -- --vendor
mixpanel-analytics` → ✅ full tier, SDK reports `__loaded`, no
version-mismatch error

feat(scripts): denied-consent egress assertion for alwaysLoad vendors (#917)

Closes #914. Stacked on #913 (Heap) — continues the monitor/integration
stack.

## Summary

The live vendor monitor previously skipped the consent phase for
`alwaysLoad` vendors with "manages consent internally; not asserted".
That left our riskiest trust assumption unverified: GTM and Mixpanel run
for **every** visitor, including users who denied consent.

The consent phase now runs a **denied-consent egress assertion** for
these vendors in an isolated browser context (so warmed caches never
contaminate the granted-consent probe):

1. Load the vendor with denied consent through the production script
loader
2. Let the real SDK initialize and attempt collection (4s quiet window)
3. Assert **zero requests to the vendor's collection endpoints** — a
blocked attempt is still a violation, the attempt proves intent
4. Assert **zero vendor cookies/localStorage** (per-vendor prefixes;
consent-state markers like Mixpanel's `__mp_opt_in_out_*` are legitimate
and excluded)

Consent-safe traffic is excluded via explicit per-vendor allow/violation
lists — Google Consent Mode's cookieless pings are safe by design, so
GTM's violation list names real collection endpoints (`/g/collect`,
doubleclick) and ad-storage cookies (`_ga*`, `_gcl*`) only.

### Live-verified

- **mixpanel-analytics** ✅ — the real SDK initializes under denied
consent, the queued `opt_out_tracking` replays (with
`opt_out_tracking_by_default` in init options, the configuration our
docs recommend for alwaysLoad usage), and the probe observes zero
collection requests and clean storage

lands as a repo secret (placeholder ids 404 before tags can run)

Enterprises running RudderStack want the vendor-sanctioned CMP flow
instead of losing pre-consent events to the blocked load. This adds it
as an **explicit opt-in**, keeping blocked-load the default:

```ts

  writeKey: 'WRITE_KEY',
  dataPlaneUrl: 'https://example.dataplane.rudderstack.com',

      measurement: ['product-analytics'],
```

'custom', allowedConsentIds, deniedConsentIds } })`, partitioned from
the category mapping; the initial signal is queued before load

buffer and deliver once consent is granted; users who never consent get

storage `'session'` for session stitching) — documented tradeoff

Fix Microsoft Clarity consent bootstrap (#898)

## Summary

- remove the pre-load `window.clarity.v` marker from the Microsoft
Clarity stub so Clarity's own loader no longer treats c15t as a
duplicate install
- switch c15t's Clarity synchronization to Consent V2 with `ad_Storage`
and `analytics_Storage`
- map c15t `marketing` consent to Clarity `ad_Storage` and `measurement`
consent to Clarity `analytics_Storage`
- update unit/e2e coverage to assert Consent V2 is queued before the
Clarity tag loads and that the stub does not expose `v`

## Context

Microsoft's current `clarity-js` queue processor exits early when
`window.clarity.v` is already present. c15t was setting `v: "0.7.0"` on
the bootstrap stub before `https://www.clarity.ms/tag/{id}` ran, so the
Microsoft tag loader detected a duplicate install and skipped loading
`clarity.js`. That left customers with the Clarity tag request but no
`clarity.js`, no collect calls, and no dashboard data.

Microsoft's implementation sets `window.clarity.v` only after the real
runtime replaces the queued stub, so the c15t stub should only queue
calls. This also updates the helper to use Clarity Consent V2 instead of
the older boolean consent API.

Fix consent dedupe race without a schema change (#863)

## Summary

Fixes #861 by making consent creation idempotent for concurrent
identical `POST /subjects` requests, without a database schema change or
migration.

The issue's reproduction uses the same subject, domain, policy, and
`givenAt`. Those requests now derive the same `consent.id`, so the
existing primary-key constraint rejects the losing insert and the
handler returns the winner.

## Scope: identical requests and double taps

The backend deduplicates the issue's exact case: identical request
bodies with the same `givenAt`. Requests with different timestamps
remain distinct consent events.

c15t's client store now also coalesces concurrent saves with the same
intent while the first save is in flight. This covers a real double tap
through the banner/headless store even though two independently
generated requests would otherwise receive different `Date.now()`
values. Direct API callers, separate tabs, or separate processes that
intentionally submit different `givenAt` values are not merged.

Network retries and offline-queue replay already preserve the request
body, so they are protected by the deterministic primary key.

## What changed

- Derive `consent.id` from tenant, subject, domain, policy, and
`givenAt`.
- Recover unique conflicts outside the transaction, because PostgreSQL
aborts the transaction after a failed statement.
- Coalesce concurrent identical banner and policy-consent saves in the
core store.
- Use one indexed primary-key lookup for current submissions.
- Retain a field-based compatibility lookup only when the submitted
timestamp could belong to a row written by a pre-deterministic-ID
process.
- Remove the redundant in-transaction consent re-check; the primary-key
insert and bounded retry loop provide the exclusion.
- Reject timestamps outside JavaScript's representable `Date` range
before calling `toISOString()`.

## Why not a `dedupeKey` column

FumaDB schemas are immutable and migrations are generated by diffing
versions. Editing schema `2.0.0` in place generates no DDL for a
database already at `2.0.0`, while the runtime then queries a column
that does not exist. Existing deployments would fail consent reads and
writes.

The primary key already exists and is uniquely enforced on every
supported database, so using it avoids a migration and a production
index build.

## Compatibility and ordering notes

- Existing rows retain random IDs. Old, backdated, and future-skewed
submissions use the compatibility lookup after an ID miss.
- The time-ordered portion of a deterministic consent ID reflects client
`givenAt`, not server insertion time. Pre-2023-11-14 timestamps share
the zero timestamp prefix. No current consent handler orders or
paginates by ID; this should be revisited before introducing ID-based
cursors.
- Fractional epoch-millisecond values remain accepted. Only values that
cannot be represented by `Date` are rejected.

## Validation

- PostgreSQL/PGlite HTTP integration: real FumaDB migration, real
`23505` primary-key conflict, rollback recovery, concurrent submissions,
retry, and distinct timestamps.
- Core store unit coverage for concurrent banner and policy-consent
double taps.
- Backend unit coverage for the one-read hot path, legacy fallback,
bounded retries, and conflict recovery.
- Schema unit coverage for representable bounds, including fractional
and negative timestamps.
- `c15t`: 507 tests passed.
- `@c15t/backend`: 546 tests passed.
- `@c15t/schema`: 95 tests passed.
- Type checks and Biome passed for all affected packages.

No database migration is required.

Clamp future consent time to server time (#862)

## Summary

Clamp `POST /subjects` consent `givenAt` timestamps that are more than
five minutes ahead of server time to the server's current time.

This PR is stacked on #863 and should merge after it. It does not close
a GitHub issue; the future-clock-skew bug was found during review of the
consent deduplication path.

## Why

`givenAt` comes from the client's clock. A skewed device can report
consent arbitrarily far in the future, distorting the audit record and
pushing `validUntil = givenAt + expiryDays` out indefinitely.

Rejecting the request would prevent the affected user from recording
consent, so the backend records server time instead.

## Interaction with #863

The recorded timestamp changes on every retry because it uses current
server time. Consent identity therefore derives from the client's
original claim, while the clamped value is stored and returned. This
keeps a skewed client's retries idempotent.

#863 now independently rejects timestamps outside JavaScript's
representable `Date` range, so merging #863 first cannot turn `givenAt:
1e18` into a new `toISOString()` 500.

## What changed

- Clamp timestamps more than five minutes ahead of server time before
deriving `validUntil`.
- Preserve the original client claim as `metadata.clientGivenAt`.
- Derive identity from the original claim so retries remain stable.
- Read conflict winners by deterministic primary key.
- Synchronize local `consentInfo.time` from the timestamp returned by
the server, avoiding disagreement between local state and the returned
consent.
- Continue accepting fractional, negative, and past timestamps when they
are representable by JavaScript `Date`.

## Deferred scope

Past timestamps remain unbounded because choosing a lower bound requires
a product/compliance decision about legitimate offline replay.
Follow-up: #936.

The deterministic ID's time prefix reflects the client's claimed
timestamp rather than server insertion time. No current consent endpoint
orders by ID.

## Validation

- Handler unit coverage for clamping, the tolerance boundary, past
replay, metadata, `validUntil`, stable retry identity, and conflict
recovery.
- Core store unit coverage that local consent time follows the
server-recorded value.
- The PostgreSQL integration from #863 runs on the stacked branch.
- Full stack: 546 backend tests, 507 core tests, and 95 schema tests
passed.
- Type checks and Biome passed for all affected packages.

No database migration is required.

fix(react): apply CSP nonce to injected styles and scripts (#949)

Closes #948

## Problem

c15t injects its theme tokens as `<style id="c15t-theme">`, and that
element carried no nonce. Under a nonce-based Content Security Policy
the browser refuses it:

```
Refused to apply inline style because it violates the following Content Security Policy directive: "style-src-elem ..."
```

The only workaround was allowing `'unsafe-inline'`.

It was worse than a missed prop: `nonce` was not part of the provider
options at all — not in `CoreOptions`, `UIOptions`,
`CommonInlineStoreOptions`, or `ConsentManagerContentOptions` — so a
value passed there was dropped at the type boundary before it could
reach a DOM node.

## Fix

A single top-level `nonce` option, forwarded to everything c15t injects.

```tsx
<ConsentManagerProvider options={{ mode: 'offline', nonce }}>
  {children}
</ConsentManagerProvider>
```

**Theme stylesheet**
- `nonce?: string` on `CommonInlineStoreOptions` (public,
framework-facing — the options reference table renders from it) and on
`StoreConfig` in core. The core declaration is enough on its own for
three things: `StoreOptions extends Partial<StoreConfig>` accepts it,
`StoreRuntimeState extends StoreConfig` exposes it in state, and the
existing `...storeConfigOptions` spread populates it with no extra
wiring.
- The provider passes it to the `<style>` element.

**Script loader**
- `nonce` added to the shared `ScriptLoaderOptions` bag and resolved at
the single element-creation site as `script.nonce ?? options?.nonce`, so
a per-script value still wins.
- Threaded from state at both call sites (`updateScripts` and
`reloadScript`), which covers scripts declared in provider options *and*
scripts registered later via `setScripts`.

Without this second part a strict-CSP app hits the identical wall on
`script-src` the moment it uses the script loader, and today's only
answer is repeating the nonce on every script entry.

## Tests

- `provider-nonce.test.tsx` — the original issue repro (verified failing
before the fix) plus a negative case. Asserts via `styleEl.nonce` rather
than `getAttribute`, since browsers hide the content attribute once a
policy is live.
- 6 script-loader tests: 3 unit (loader default, per-script override,
neither set) and 3 store-level integration proving `options.nonce`
reaches the injected element.

`check-types` passes repo-wide. Full suites green: core 519, react 397,
plus ui and nextjs.

## Docs

A shared "Content Security Policy" section imported into the React and
Next provider pages, including a Next-specific middleware → `headers()`
→ provider example. The stale per-script CSP advice in
`next/script-loader.mdx` now points at the provider option.

## Notes for review

- The `nonce` option covers elements c15t injects. It does not cover
inline `style="..."` attributes, which CSP governs through
`style-src-attr` — a directive that ignores nonces entirely. Documented
as a caveat, since the reporter's policy sets `style-src-attr 'self'`.
- Unrelated and not addressed here: `noStyle: true` does not currently
suppress the theme `<style>` element; the provider renders it
unconditionally. Happy to file that separately.

ci: cache Playwright browsers and the Turborepo local cache (#953)

Stacked on #952 — both PRs rewrite overlapping parts of `ci.yml`. Base
retargets to `canary` automatically once #952 merges.

## Why

Measured on CI run `30625455595`, nothing in this repo's CI is cached:

- `Remote caching disabled`, `Cached: 0 cached, 47 total` — every turbo
task cold on every PR.
- `actions/cache/restore` for Playwright is the **only** cache action in
the repo. Nothing saves it, so it reported `Cache not found for input
keys` and re-downloaded Chromium — **32s** of the test job's 171s.
- No `.turbo` persistence to substitute for the disabled remote cache.

Note this is unrelated to Turborepo's Git worktree cache sharing, which
is already working — that redirects a linked worktree's cache to the
main worktree and is local-only. CI does a fresh clone, not a worktree,
so it contributes nothing here.

## Changes

**Playwright.** `actions/cache/restore` → `actions/cache`, so the
post-step actually writes the key. Re-keyed on the resolved Playwright
version instead of `hashFiles('bun.lock')` — browsers only change when
Playwright does, and lockfile churn was invalidating them on every
unrelated dependency bump (this repo bumps the lockfile often;
affected-scoping in #952 makes lockfile changes a full run anyway).

**Turborepo local cache.** All three jobs restore `.turbo/cache`
read-only. The **test job is the single writer** — it builds every
package as a dependency of `test`, so its cache is the most complete,
and one writer avoids concurrent-save conflicts on the same key.

Saves are gated to `push` only. PR runs restore read-only, which keeps
them from churning the 10GB repo budget and matches the posture already
chosen for `TURBO_TOKEN`. GitHub scopes caches per branch, so a PR
cannot write into canary's scope regardless.

**Pruning.** Restored entries carry into each save, so the cache would
grow without bound across pushes and evict everything else. It's pruned
newest-first to a 1GB ceiling before saving.

## Testing

- actionlint clean, including its shellcheck pass over the prune script.
- Prune pipeline tested against real files: 20 x 100KB with staggered
mtimes and a 1MB limit → exactly 10 survivors, the 10 newest. Correct
ordering and cutoff.
- Verified the resolved step graph: 3 read-only restores, save gated to
`push`, prune non-fatal.

**Not verified locally:** the prune uses `find -printf` and `xargs -r`,
which are GNU-only — no GNU findutils or working container runtime on
this machine, so only the `sort | awk | xargs` half ran here. Two
deliberate mitigations: the prune runs on **every** event rather than
only on pushes, so this PR's own CI exercises it; and it is
`continue-on-error: true`, so a failure means a larger cache, never a
failed build. Worth reading its log line on this PR before merge.

The **save** path still cannot be exercised until this is on a push to
`canary` — check the first post-merge run.

## Expected effect

~32s from Playwright plus cold-build savings on the test job. Roughly 3
min → ~2 min. Modest, because the repo is already fast; the point is
that both were straightforward gaps.

## Separately

`Failed to restore: Cache service responded with 400` appears in **Setup
Bun** on all three jobs. That is `oven-sh/setup-bun`'s own bundled
cache, not `actions/cache` — the pinned `actions/cache` v4.3.0 reported
a clean miss with no 400. Not touched here.

ci: fix coverage reporting and dedupe the coverage workflow (#955)

Stacked on #953 (which is stacked on #952). Bases retarget automatically
as each merges.

## The bug

Coverage reporting has failed on **every run since at least
2026-07-27**. I traced it: it is a typo, not a path or artifact problem.

The `report` job succeeds and produces a perfectly correct matrix —
verified against a real run:

```
coverage-artifacts/packages/logger/coverage/coverage-summary.json
"summary_path": "coverage-artifacts/packages/logger/coverage/coverage-summary.json"
```

All 11 matrix jobs then fail at the reporting action with `ENOENT` on
`/home/runner/work/c15t/c15t/coverage/coverage-summary.json` — the
action's **default** path. The workflow passed:

```yaml
json_summary_path: ...   # underscores
json_final_path: ...
```

but reading `action.yml` at the pinned SHA, the inputs are
**hyphenated**:

```
json-summary-path
json-final-path
```

GitHub Actions silently discards unknown inputs, so the action never
received the paths and fell back to its default. `name` happens to be a
real input, which is why the job titles looked correct and masked it.

## Changes

- **Fix the input names.** The actual bug.
- **Pass `pr-number` explicitly.** `workflow_run` carries no
`pull_request` payload, so the action cannot work out which PR to
comment on — its `pr-number` default is empty. Resolved from
`workflow_run.pull_requests`, with a fallback lookup by head SHA because
fork PRs arrive with that array empty.
- **Replace the blanket `continue-on-error`** on the artifact download
(added in #952) with an explicit existence probe. CodeRabbit's point on
#952 was fair: unconditional tolerance masks genuine download failures.
Now an absent artifact skips cleanly and a real failure still fails
loudly.
- **Declare the scopes both jobs need.** Specifying `permissions` sets
every unlisted scope to `none`, and the jobs need `actions: read` to
reach the triggering run's artifacts and `contents: read` for the
head-SHA lookup.
- **Delete `ci-coverage.yml`** — byte-identical to `coverage-report.yml`
apart from one stale comment. Both were named "Report Coverage" and both
fired on every CI completion, doubling compute and PR comments.
- Fix the "afterwards" spelling static analysis flagged on #952.

## Testing

- actionlint clean across all workflows, including its shellcheck pass
over the two new script steps.
- **Every input we pass validated against the action's real
`action.yml`** at the pinned SHA: `name`, `json-summary-path`,
`json-final-path`, `pr-number` all ✓. This is the check that would have
caught the original bug.
- Confirmed `canary` has no branch protection, so removing a workflow
drops no required check.
- Confirmed the two coverage workflows differed only by one comment line
before deleting one.

## Caveat on verification — please read before merging

**None of this can be exercised by CI on this PR.** `workflow_run`
workflows always run the **default branch's** copy of their own
definition, so any change here only takes effect once it is on `canary`.
That is also why the #952 artifact fix still shows red on these PRs.

Because each iteration costs a full merge cycle rather than a push, I
front-loaded robustness rather than fixing only the typo and seeing what
happened next — hence resolving `pr-number` and the permission scopes in
the same change.

**After merge, check the first coverage run for:** `Resolved pull
request: <n>`, `Matching artifacts: <n>`, and an actual coverage comment
on the PR. If the comment still does not appear, `pr-number` resolution
is the next thing to look at.

fix(scripts): seed PostHog snippet init queue so array.js installs (#982)

Fixes #981.

## What broke

PostHog JS 1.410.2 added a duplicate-loader guard. When `window.posthog`
already exists, `array.js` only installs its runtime if `posthog._i` is
an array. The c15t bootstrap stub had no `_i`, so the CDN script
returned successfully but left the noop stub installed and every event
was dropped.

## Minimal fix

Seed the pending-init registry as `{ _i: [] }`. This is the smallest
change that satisfies the upstream loader guard while preserving the
existing c15t lifecycle: the real SDK installs first, then the existing
load callback calls `posthog.init(...)`.

This PR intentionally contains only the hotfix, its regression test, and
a patch changeset. The unrelated Turbo cache change was moved to #994.

in flight.

instanceName]` tuple in `_i`

fix(backend): support native WebView app schemes in trustedOrigins

Origins such as `capacitor://localhost` (the default iOS Capacitor origin),
`ionic://localhost`, and custom `iosScheme` values could not be used as
trusted origins.

`normalizeOrigin` prefixed any entry lacking an http(s)/ws(s) scheme with
`http://`, so `capacitor://localhost` parsed as the hostname `capacitor`.
That collapsed every `capacitor://` origin onto a single host, meaning a
trusted `capacitor://localhost` also trusted `capacitor://evil.com`. The
two origin matchers additionally disagreed, since `isOriginTrusted`
ignored schemes entirely while the CORS layer collapsed them.

Add a shared `app-scheme` helper used by both matchers. An entry naming a
non-web scheme is pinned to it and matched on scheme and host; entries
with no scheme or an http(s)/ws(s) scheme stay protocol-agnostic and match
exactly as before, so existing configurations are unaffected.

fix(backend): match app-scheme hosts verbatim in isOriginTrusted

`www.` was stripped from both sides of the exact-hostname comparison
regardless of scheme, so a trusted `capacitor://localhost` also matched
the distinct origin `capacitor://www.localhost`. That contradicted the
exact scheme-and-host guarantee and disagreed with `createCORSOptions`,
which already rejected it.

Apply the `www.` equivalence only to entries with no app scheme, leaving
the web-domain convention unchanged.
docs: tighten app-scheme trusted-origins changeset

fix(backend): correct www handling in CORS origin matching

`*.example.com` rejected `https://www.example.com` while allowing every
other subdomain, and a schemeless `www.example.com` entry matched nothing
at all — neither the apex nor itself.

Both came from stripping `www.` off the incoming origin in
`normalizeOrigin`. That turned `www.example.com` into the apex
`example.com`, which a `*.` wildcard deliberately excludes, and it left
schemeless trusted entries keeping a `www.` the origin could never carry.

Stop stripping `www.` from the origin and apply the equivalence to the
trusted list instead, which now holds both the apex and `www.` form of
every entry. Wildcard entries are skipped, since they already cover every
subdomain and `www.*.example.com` could never match.

fix(backend): keep wildcard entries out of www apex derivation

Stripping `www.` to derive an apex widened any entry that carried a
wildcard: `www.*` became the allow-all `*`, and `www.*.example.com`
became `*.example.com`, granting arbitrary subdomains.

Skip apex derivation for any entry containing `*`, not just those
starting with `*.`. Such entries are still added verbatim, where they
match nothing, as before.

fix(backend): correct www handling in CORS origin matching (#1013)

> 📚 Stacked on #1012. Review that one first — this branch contains only
the `www` fix.

## Overview

Two trusted-origin configurations silently failed to match the origins
they should. Both are pre-existing and unrelated to #1012; I confirmed
them against an unmodified `origin/canary` worktree.

| Trusted entry | Origin | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| `*.example.com` | `https://www.example.com` | **null** | allowed |
| `*.example.com` | `https://api.example.com` | allowed | allowed |
| `*.example.com` | `https://example.com` (apex) | null | null |
| `www.example.com` | `https://example.com` | **null** | allowed |
| `www.example.com` | `https://www.example.com` | **null** | allowed |

So `*.example.com` allowed every subdomain *except* `www` — the one
people hit first — and a schemeless `www.example.com` entry matched
nothing at all, not even itself.

Both trace to one line: `normalizeOrigin` stripped `www.` off the
**incoming origin**. That turned `www.example.com` into the apex
`example.com`, which a `*.` wildcard deliberately excludes. And because
the schemeless branch returns before that strip, a schemeless trusted
entry kept a `www.` prefix the normalized origin could never carry.

## Related Issue

Fixes # (issue)

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)

## Implementation Details

### Key Changes

1. **`normalizeOrigin`** — no longer strips `www.`; returns
`host[:port]` as-is. The catch-branch fallback strips only the protocol.
2. **`expandWithWWW`** — adds both the apex and the `www.` form of every
entry, whichever was configured. Wildcard entries are skipped: they
already cover every subdomain, and a `www.*.example.com` entry could
never match anything.

### Technical Notes

Moving the equivalence entirely onto the trusted list is what makes both
cases work from one change. The origin is now compared verbatim, so
wildcard matching sees the real hostname.

`isOriginTrusted` already handled both cases correctly, so this also
removes a disagreement between the two matchers.

## Testing

### Test Plan

- [x] Scenario 1: `www` from a wildcard-only config

  ```ts

createCORSOptions(['https://*.example.com']).origin('https://www.example.com');
  ```

  ✓ Expected: echoes the origin (previously `null`)

- [x] Scenario 2: schemeless `www` entry accepts both forms

  ```ts
  createCORSOptions(['www.c15t.com']).origin('http://c15t.com');
  createCORSOptions(['www.c15t.com']).origin('http://www.c15t.com');
  ```

  ✓ Expected: both echo the origin (previously both `null`)

- [x] Scenario 3: malformed wildcards stay contained

  ```ts
  createCORSOptions(['www.*']).origin('https://evil.com');

createCORSOptions(['www.*.example.com']).origin('https://evil.example.com');
  ```

  ✓ Expected: `null` for both

### Edge Cases

- [x] Security: this **widens** matching, so it got the most scrutiny.
Wildcards still exclude the apex (`*.example.com` ✗ `example.com`),
near-miss hosts are still rejected (`example.com` ✗ `notexample.com`,
`*.example.com` ✗ `badexample.com`, `example.com.evil.com`), and only

chore: add GitHub issue label taxonomy (#1019)

## Overview

Adds a `labels.yml` source of truth for GitHub labels and points the
issue templates at names that actually exist.

The old set mixed emoji kind labels (`✨ feature`, `🐛 bug`) with template
names that did not match (`enhancement`, `documentation`,
`needs-triage`). New issues often landed unlabeled. This replaces that
with:

- **Kind:** `bug`, `feature`, `docs` — applied by the matching template
- **Area:** product surface (`area:react`, `area:nuxt`, `area:scripts`,
…), not package folder. v3 is one kernel plus thin adapters; Nuxt lives
in `packages/vue`, React Router is Remix not TanStack.
- **State:** maintainer-applied (`needs-repro`, `needs-approval`, `help
wanted`, …)
- **Unlabeled** means untriaged — there is no `needs-triage` label

`from_name` records the emoji renames so a labeler action can migrate
existing issues in place.

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

1. Sync live repo labels from `labels.yml` (create / rename).
2. Retarget the 14 open issues and 3 product PRs onto the new areas. Do
not backfill closed issues.

Suggested open-issue mapping is in the review discussion if useful.
